messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For Amir, the moment that shattered everything happened on a Tuesday evening. He had been the first paramedic on scene after a multi-car collision on the interstate, and he had recognized the car. It was his brother-in-law’s sedan, crumpled against the guardrail. Amir had pulled him from the wreckage, working with a calm he no longer recognizes in himself, applying pressure to the wounds that would not stop bleeding. He remembers the antiseptic smell of the hospital bay where he finally handed him off to the trauma team, the sharp chemical scent that now seems to follow him everywhere. He remembers the terror in his own chest, a feeling that did not leave when the doctors told him his brother-in-law would survive. What Amir cannot remember, no matter how hard he tries, are the minutes between recognizing the car and getting him onto the stretcher. There are gaps in his memory that feel like missing pieces of himself, and when the memory does come back—which it does, without warning—it returns in full, vivid color, every smell and sound and sensation arriving at once, as if he is still there on the asphalt with blood on his gloves. The terror that grips him in those moments is the same terror he felt then, undiminished by time.

In the weeks and months that followed, Amir became convinced that he had permanently changed for the worse. He could feel it in his bones. Before the accident, he had trusted his instincts, his hands, his ability to stay calm under pressure. Now he cannot rely on himself. He replays the scene obsessively, searching for something he could have done differently, and the conclusion is always the same: he should have protected his brother-in-law, and he failed. This belief has settled into him like a weight. He tries hard not to think about it, pushing the memories away when they surface, but suppression only seems to make them return more forcefully. So he has adopted another strategy: he throws himself into work. He volunteers for extra shifts, takes the most difficult calls, fills every quiet moment with tasks. Overworking keeps his mind occupied, but it also means he is constantly exposed to the very things that trigger him. Visible injuries on strangers—a gash on a child’s arm, a wound being bandaged—send him reeling. He sees the faces of victims he has treated, unbidden, at the worst possible moments. And the smell of the hospital, the antiseptic that hangs in every corridor, has become a permanent part of his sensory landscape, a reminder he cannot escape.

At home, his wife has noticed the changes. He reacts with alarm when she touches him unexpectedly, sometimes flinching or pulling away before he can stop himself. He has started choosing where to sit in every room based on how safe or protected he feels—his back to a wall, a clear view of the door, a position from which no one can approach him unseen. He has difficulty concentrating, finding that his mind drifts mid-conversation, that he loses the thread of television shows, that he cannot focus on the dinner table talk that used to ground him. He has stopped wanting to go to work, though he goes anyway, because the thought of staying home with nothing to occupy his hands feels worse. The avoidance is not a choice he makes consciously; it is a reflex. He dreads the start of every shift, and yet he cannot imagine stopping, because stopping would mean sitting still with what he carries.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was not the flashbacks or the fear or the sleepless nights. It was a moment at his daughter’s birthday party, when he saw a small scrape on her knee and felt his chest seize, his vision narrow, his mouth go dry. He excused himself and sat in the bathroom for ten minutes, trying to breathe. He realized then that he could no longer trust himself to be present for the people he loved. He is afraid that the damage is permanent, that he will never feel like himself again. But he is also hoping, in a quiet way he does not yet know how to put into words, that someone can help him find a way back.
